passage:
The clip of Hafsa forgetting her lines in the school play had been shared two thousand times by Thursday. In the corridor, students from other classes smirked. In the classroom, phones lit up as she walked in. Hafsa took her seat and stared at the desk, her eyes hot. She couldn't explain that nerves had taken her voice; who would listen?

By lunch she had stopped answering messages. She told the teacher she had a stomach ache and sat on the library floor between the shelves. Jasleen found her there. “I'm not going to say anything clever,” Jasleen said. “I just didn't want you alone.” Hafsa nodded. Later Jasleen walked her to the counsellor, who listened, said none of it was Hafsa's fault, and phoned her mother that same afternoon.

qa.q: How many times had the clip been shared by Thursday?
qa.a: The clip had been shared two thousand times by Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa stop answering messages by lunch?
qa.a: Hafsa felt exposed and ashamed and could not explain what had happened, so hiding felt safer.

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen make that helped Hafsa?
qa.a: Jasleen sat with Hafsa without offering advice and later walked Hafsa to the counsellor.

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been thinking on finding Hafsa on the library floor?
qa.a: Jasleen probably felt worried and protective, unsure what to say, and chose simply to stay.

grounding: A teenager is flooded with mocking messages after a mistake goes viral, feels exposed and ashamed, and is helped by a peer and the school counsellor.

Dear Sachin Sir,

I'm writing because I can't say this out loud. Last Friday I mixed up the answer in the quiz, and a classmate filmed it. Now the clip is on the class group, and people from other sections send me laughing lines. I keep reading them at night. I don't want to go to school on Monday. I keep thinking everyone has seen it, and nobody would believe I just froze.

Please don't tell anyone. I feel so stupid.

Rajni

P.S. (5 p.m.) I sent this at seven this morning. At lunch you came to the library, sat down and told me none of this is my fault, and that the principal must know so it can be stopped. You also phoned my mother this afternoon, and the group has been told to delete the clip.

qa.q: At what time did Rajni send the email?
qa.a: Rajni sent the email at seven that morning.

qa.q: Why did Rajni ask Sachin Sir not to tell anyone?
qa.a: Rajni felt stupid and ashamed and feared more attention, even though the email itself was a request for help.

qa.q: What did Sachin Sir do the same day that helped Rajni?
qa.a: Sachin Sir came to the library, said none of it was Rajni's fault, informed the principal and phoned Rajni's mother.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sachin Sir to open an email like this at the start of the day?
qa.a: Sachin Sir probably felt concern and urgency, knowing a student was frightened to come to school and needed action that day.

grounding: A teenager flooded with mocking messages after a mistake goes viral feels ashamed and unable to explain, and writes to a trusted adult.

I'm Nandini, and last year I had the worst week of my life because of one wrong answer.
At the inter-school quiz, on stage, I said the capital of Australia was Sydney. Someone filmed it. By evening it was everywhere, with music and a clown face. My friend Omkar forwarded it to me with “sorry, it's in every group”.
Hundreds of messages. Strangers. People from my own class. I couldn't explain. Nobody would listen anyway.
I stayed in my room the next day and told Mummy I had a stomach ache. I was too scared to go out.
That evening she came in, saw my phone and my face, and sat on the bed. She said, “This is not your fault.” We reported the posts together, and she called my class teacher that same night.

qa.q: What answer did Nandini give on stage?
qa.a: Nandini said the capital of Australia was Sydney.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel during the pile-on?
qa.a: Nandini felt exposed, ashamed and scared, unable to explain and too afraid to leave the room.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed, sat with Nandini, said it wasn't Nandini's fault, reported the posts and called the class teacher the same night.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt forwarding the video?
qa.a: Omkar probably felt uneasy and sorry, warning Nandini that it was already everywhere.

grounding: A teenager recalls being flooded with mocking messages after a mistake went viral, feeling exposed and afraid to leave home.

School counsellor's note, Tuesday.
Sumit, Class 11, has not come to school since Friday, when a video of him tripping on stage during the annual day dance was shared widely online, with mocking edits.
This morning, his friend Kiran came to me. Kiran said Sumit had messaged, “I can't face anyone. Everyone's seen it.”
I called Sumit's mother at once. She said he has barely left his room. I spoke with Sumit on the phone; he was quiet and ashamed, and said he couldn't face anyone at school. I told him none of this was his fault.
Today I informed the principal, arranged to visit Sumit at home this evening with his class teacher, and asked the IT team to report the posts.

qa.q: Since when has Sumit not come to school?
qa.a: He has not come to school since Friday.

qa.q: How did Sumit seem to feel on the phone?
qa.a: He seemed quiet and ashamed, too afraid to face anyone after the video.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take, and why are they right?
qa.a: The counsellor called his mother at once, spoke to Sumit, told him it wasn't his fault, informed the principal and planned a home visit that evening, so he isn't left alone with it.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt coming to the counsellor?
qa.a: Kiran probably felt worried about a friend and relieved to pass it to an adult who could help.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager flooded with mocking posts after a stage mistake, ashamed and afraid to leave his room.

Sunday, 9:30 pm
I can't stop shaking. The clip of me crying after the debate loss is now a meme. “When you lose one debate and it's the end of the world.” Salma sent it to me with a sad face; she says it's in ten groups.
People I don't even know are commenting. Someone put my face on a crying baby. I tried to explain that my grandmother was in hospital that day, but nobody reads replies.
I don't want to go to school tomorrow. I don't want to go anywhere.
Mumma came in at nine and saw me. She sat on the bed and held me, and said it wasn't my fault. We reported every post together. She's calling the principal first thing tomorrow, and she said we'll go in together.
Ankita

qa.q: How many groups does Salma say the meme is in?
qa.a: Salma says it's in ten groups.

qa.q: How is Ankita feeling tonight?
qa.a: Ankita feels exposed, ashamed and overwhelmed, shaking and not wanting to go anywhere.

qa.q: What did Mumma do that helped Ankita right away?
qa.a: She held Ankita, said it wasn't Ankita's fault, reported the posts that night and planned to call the principal first thing.

qa.q: How might Salma feel having sent the meme?
qa.a: She might feel worried and a bit guilty, wanting to warn a friend but also spreading it further.

grounding: A teenager writes about becoming a meme after a moment of crying went viral, feeling exposed and unable to explain.
